## Riding/Wearing Shoes <note>original: 乘履</note>

> **Biography of Dongfang Shuo**: Emperor Wu said to Shuo, "I wish for my favorites to never age, is this possible?" Shuo replied, "Your servant can achieve this." The Emperor asked, "What medicine must be taken?" Shuo said, "In the northeast, there is an herb of immortality. When I was a child, someone led me to retrieve this herb, but we were separated by a red spring and could not cross. That person gave me one shoe, and I went against the current of the spring to obtain and eat it."

## Riding on a Shoe
<gloss>Note: Now those with teeth</gloss>

> **The Biography of Dongfang Shuo**: Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty addressed Shuo, saying: "I wish to make my favorites and those I love stay young forever. Is this possible?" Shuo replied: "I am capable of achieving this." The Emperor asked: "What medicine should they take?" Shuo said: "In the lands to the northeast, there grows a divine fungus <term>zhicao</term> <gloss>immortality grass</gloss>. When I was a child, someone led me to gather this plant, but we were separated by the Red Spring and could not cross. That person gave me a single shoe; I then waded up through the spring, reached the plant, and ate it."

...the affairs of King Wu, and the music of the Great Martial Dance <note>original: "大武"</note> represents the affairs of King Wu. Both are intended as representations. However, the preface here says "Performing the Great Martial Dance, the dance representing the martial deeds" in the section on the "Wu" poem <note>refers to the *Zhou Song* poem "Wu"</note>. It cannot repeat the phrase "performing the representation," so it indicates the name of the music by saying "performing the Great Martial Dance." In reality, the music of the Great Martial Dance also acts as a representation. Therefore, the *Liji* <note>Book of Rites</note>—in the chapters "Wen Wang Shi Zi," "Ming Tang Wei," and "Ji Tong"—all say, "Singing 'Qing Miao' <note>a poem in the Zhou Song</note> while ascending, and playing the *Xiang* <note>a type of dance music</note> with lower-register pipes." *Xiang* and *Qing Miao* are paired, meaning both are poems. Thus, the annotation on "Ming Tang Wei" explains that the *Xiang* refers to the "Wu" poem of the *Zhou Song*. It means the "Wu" poem is the *Xiang*, making it clear that the section of the Great Martial Dance is also a representation. However, the text of the *Liji* separately mentions "dancing the Great Martial Dance" after mentioning the pipes. This means the music for the "Wu" poem is also a representation.

<summary>This passage clarifies the terminology used to describe the "Great Martial Dance" music and its relationship to the "Wu" poem within the *Zhou Song*, reconciling discrepancies between the preface and the *Book of Rites*.</summary>
<keywords>Mao Shi Zhushu, Great Martial Dance, Da Wu, Zhou Song, Liji, music, ritual, representation</keywords>

# Volume 40

### Ritual Offerings of Wine and Spirits

For the primary and associated deity positions, the <term>taizun</term> <gloss>great vessel</gloss> is filled with <term>fanqi</term> <gloss>floating wine</gloss> and <term>liqi</term> <gloss>sweet wine</gloss>. The <term>zhuzun</term> <gloss>manifest vessel</gloss> is filled with <term>angqi</term> <gloss>bubbling wine</gloss>. The <term>xizun</term> <gloss>sacrificial ox vessel</gloss> is filled with <term>tiqi</term> <gloss>reddish wine</gloss>. The <term>shanlei</term> <gloss>mountain-patterned jar</gloss> is filled with <term>xijiu</term> <gloss>aged wine</gloss>. These are placed atop the altar.

The <term>taizun</term> <gloss>great vessel</gloss> is also filled with <term>shenqi</term> <gloss>sunken wine</gloss>. The <term>shanlei</term> <gloss>mountain jars</gloss> are filled with <term>shijiu</term> <gloss>service wine</gloss> and <term>qingjiu</term> <gloss>clear wine</gloss>. These are placed below the altar.

For the subordinate sacrificial positions, the <term>zhuzun</term> <gloss>manifest vessel</gloss> is filled with <term>liqi</term> <gloss>sweet wine</gloss> and <term>angqi</term> <gloss>bubbling wine</gloss>. The <term>xizun</term> <gloss>sacrificial ox vessel</gloss> is filled with <term>shijiu</term> <gloss>service wine</gloss>.

### Grain Offerings

For both the primary and associated positions as well as the subordinate sacrifices, the <term>fu</term> <gloss>rectangular grain vessels</gloss> are filled with broomcorn millet and foxtail millet. The <term>gui</term> <gloss>round grain vessels</gloss> are filled with rice and spiked millet.

### Contents of the Ritual Baskets and Bowls

For the primary and associated positions at the <term>Fangqiu</term> <gloss>Square Mound, the Altar to Earth</gloss>, each <term>bian</term> <gloss>bamboo basket</gloss> is filled respectively with: dried salt, dried fish, dates, chestnuts, hazelnuts, water caltrops, foxnuts, dried venison, black rice cakes, white rice cakes, parched grain cakes, and bean flour cakes.

Each <term>dou</term> <gloss>wooden bowl</gloss> is filled respectively with: pickled leeks, minced meat in brine, pickled greens, minced venison, pickled celery, minced rabbit, pickled bamboo shoots, minced fish, pickled tripe, minced pork, <term>baoshi</term> <gloss>finished food vegetable stew</gloss>, and <term>sanshi</term> <gloss>grain and meat paste</gloss>.

For the subordinate sacrifices, the contents of the <term>bian</term> <gloss>bamboo baskets</gloss> exclude the parched grain cakes and bean flour cakes. The <term>dou</term> <gloss>wooden bowls</gloss> exclude the vegetable stew and the grain and meat paste.

### Ceremonial Settings

The placement of the seating mats uses crimson fabric, following the same protocol as the <term>Jiaotian</term> <gloss>Sacrifice to Heaven at the Suburban Altar</gloss>. The chariots and banners used are also the same as those used for the sacrifice to Heaven.

It specifies which vessels are used for primary versus subordinate deities and notes that the ceremonial mats and banners mirror those used in the Sacrifice to Heaven.</summary>

<margin>Thirteen, Mao’s Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Odes, Imperial Edition of the Four Treasuries</margin>

Regarding these matters, the music of the *Great Warrior* <note>original: "Dawa" 大武; refers to the ritual dance of King Wu of Zhou</note> symbolizes the deeds of King Wu. Both are forms of "Images" <note>symbolic ritual dances</note>. However, the author of the Preface here mentions the performance of the *Great Warrior* and the "Image Dance" <note>original: "Xiangwu" 象舞</note>. In the section for the *Martial* <note>original: "Wu" 武; a specific poem in the Odes</note> poem, it was not possible to repeat the word "Image," so the text specifically uses the name of the music and calls it the performance of the *Great Warrior*. In reality, the music of the *Great Warrior* is also an "Image." Therefore, the *Book of Rites* in the chapters on the Crown Prince, the Hall of Distinction, and the System of Sacrifices all state: "Sing the *Pure Temple* <note>original: "Qingmiao" 清廟</note> in the upper hall, and play the 'Image' on the flutes in the lower hall." The "Image" and the *Pure Temple* are placed in opposition, and thus both are names of poems. Therefore, the commentary on the Hall of Distinction defines "Image" as the "Martial" poem of the Odes of Zhou. By calling the poem "Martial" an "Image," it is clear that the chapter on the *Great Warrior* is also an "Image." 

However, the text of the *Record* <note>the Book of Rites</note> below the word "flute" separately mentions the performance of the *Great Warrior Dance* <note>original: "舞大武"</note>, meaning the music of the *Martial* poem is also an "Image." <note>The remaining text on this page consists of the preceding clause "but the text of the Record below the word 'flute' separately mentions the performance of the Great Warrior Dance, meaning the music of the Martial poem is also an 'Image'" repeated without variation hundreds of times.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the ritual terminology and classification of Zhou Dynasty sacrificial music, specifically identifying the Great Warrior dance and the Martial poem as synonymous with the term Image. The page contains a significant repetitive error where a single explanatory clause is printed hundreds of times.</summary>

It certainly would not work; earlier scholars believed in this theory for a reason. The <term>Zuo Zhuan</term> <gloss>Commentary of Zuo</gloss> states: "Create the seven tones to serve the five sounds." The <term>Guoyu</term> <gloss>Discourses of the States</gloss> records that when King Wu attacked the Shang, the year was in <term>Chunhuo</term> <gloss>the Quail Fire [constellation]</gloss>, the month was in <term>Tiansi</term> <gloss>the Celestial Horses [constellation]</gloss>, the sun was at the ford of <term>Ximu</term> <gloss>the Splitting Wood [constellation]</gloss>, the celestial marker was at the handle of the Dipper, and the star was at <term>Tianyuan</term> <gloss>the Celestial Turtle [constellation]</gloss>. From <term>Chun</term> to <term>Si</term>, there are seven arrangements representing the measurement of north and south, making seven in total. Regarding the sacrifice at the Ancestral Temple: The sacrifice at the temple of the Duke of Zhou is the ancestral sacrifice. Regarding the *Di* <gloss>a specific major ancestral sacrifice</gloss> at the temple of the Duke of Zhuang: Duke Zhuang of Lu usurped the rites by performing the *Di* sacrifice in his own temple. This is why the scholars say he did not use the correct ritual objects. The *Di* sacrifice is not for the purpose of posthumously honoring a distant ancestor; it is to match them with the Duke of Zhou. Regarding Duke Min: The *Di* sacrifice at his temple is called the *Di* sacrifice. It was performed at the Great Ancestral Temple in the second year following the completion of the mourning period for Duke Zhuang. This is the origin of the *Di* sacrifice in the Great Ancestral Temple. The ancient rites were largely lost, and the Zhao clan states that the *Di* sacrifice of Duke Zhuang should not have been performed. Duke Min followed the Duke of Zhou. His rituals were the ancestral ones of the Zhou Temple. The *Jia* <gloss>a combined ancestral sacrifice</gloss> is performed every three years. The *Di* sacrifice is performed every eight years. The *Zuo Zhuan* <gloss>Commentary of Zuo</gloss> records the rituals of the feudal lords. Duke Xi and Duke Xuan of Lu followed these rules. The *Di* sacrifice at the ancestral temple was based on the eight-year cycle. This serves as evidence of the ritual system of the state of Lu.

<summary>This page analyzes the historical context and ritual specifics of the *di* sacrifice as performed by the Lu state, particularly focusing on the propriety of Duke Zhuang and Duke Min's *di* sacrifices, examining whether they correctly followed Zhou Dynasty rites for honoring ancestors, and referencing various scholars like Zheng Kangcheng and Zhu Xi to clarify these complex ritual applications.</summary>

Sacrifice in the Ancestral Temple <note>literally the temple of the First Son, referring to the primary lineage temple</note> is also called the <term>Di</term> <gloss>great ancestral sacrifice</gloss> sacrifice. When sacrificing to the various dukes, they are paired with <term>Wen Wang</term> <gloss>King Wen of Zhou</gloss> and sacrificed to in the Zhou temple. A detailed investigation shows that sacrifices in the Ancestral Temple are also called <term>Di</term>. When sacrificing to the various dukes, they are paired with King Wen and sacrificed to in the Zhou temple. Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi</note> states that ancient rituals have been completely lost and cannot be fully investigated. The Great <term>Xia</term> <gloss>collective ancestral sacrifice</gloss> sacrifice is used to replace the <term>Di</term> sacrifice. In the 8th year of Duke Zhuang, there was a sacrifice in the Zhou temple, and Duke Xi necessarily paired it with the Zhou temple. Why did he not do this in the Great Temple <note>the temple of the founding ancestor of the State of Lu</note>? Because Duke Xi had his own years and numbers <note>his own place in the generational order</note> which all combined to make it so.

The scholar Zheng Kangcheng <note>Zheng Xuan</note> cited the events of the 8th year to prove that the State of Lu had a Zhou temple, saying that they retroactively included King Wen. Regarding the 8th year of Duke Xi and the events of Duke Xuan, when the mourning period was completed, a <term>Di</term> sacrifice was held in the Great Temple. Every three years there is one <term>Di</term> sacrifice. Therefore, in the 2nd year of Duke Xi, there was a Great <term>Di</term> in the Great Temple, which refers to the 2nd year of Duke Min <note>referring to the transition of the tablet</note>. Because the mourning for Duke Min was finished, his tablet was moved to the ancestral temple and sacrificed to. This is called the <term>Xia</term> sacrifice.

Furthermore, Zheng Kangcheng cited the Son of Heaven and the Feudal Lords, saying that after the mourning period is over, the <term>Xia</term> is held, followed by the <term>Di</term>. This follows the commentary of Master Zuo <note>Zuo Qiuming</note>. Since the <term>Xia</term> is a collective sacrifice, the <term>Di</term> is used as a replacement. Thus, everything follows the Great Temple, where they collectively partake in the sacrificial offerings.

As for the State of Lu, they possessed the Zhou Temple to retroactively honor King Wen, and they paired him with the Duke of Zhou <note>the first lord of Lu</note>. The various ancestral tablets could not be shifted from their constant positions. It is said that Duke Zhuang clearly used the ritual objects of the Son of Heaven. Not only did he retroactively honor King Wen, but he also paired him with the Duke of Zhou. Mr. Zhao <note>Zhao Pengfei</note> stated that Duke Zhuang did not retroactively pair them, therefore the text says Duke Zhuang committed an act of arrogance in his own temple. By practicing these rituals, he did not retroactively pair the ancestors.

Furthermore, Mr. Zhao, known as Boxun, said: The fact that Lu did not use the <term>Di</term> sacrifice was because it belonged to the Temple of the Duke of Zhou and reached up to King Wen. How can one be certain that the <term>Di</term> sacrifice of Duke Min for Duke Zhuang necessarily involved a retroactive pairing, and further, that it necessarily involved a collective offering?

A son of a wealthy family <note>original: 金之子, literally "child of gold"</note> does not ride near the crossbar of a carriage. A sage ruler does not take risks or seek luck through dangerous means. Now Your Majesty gallops through unpredictable mountains; should the horse be startled or the carriage break, even if Your Majesty holds your own life lightly, what of the High Ancestral Temple and the Empress Dowager? The Emperor then ceased his actions. <note>This passage quotes a memorial advising a ruler against reckless behavior.</note>

Annotation: Ru Chun says, the speed of the horse is like a flash.

In the Biography of Liu Rengui in the History of the Tang Dynasty <note>original: 唐書</note>, see the note under the first phrase.

In the Biography of Li Gang in the History of the Song Dynasty <note>original: 宋史</note>, an order stated: How can we, because of one rebelling general, flee at the first sign of trouble and show fear to the enemy? If the Liao Dynasty retreats and cowers, and if this plan is carried out, then after the carriage returns <note>original: 回馭</note>, the people's morale will be shaken and no one will have a firm will. The spirit of the soldiers will wither, and none will have the heart to fight.

Also see the note under the third section in the Biography of Chen Hongjin.

Those who ride upon the cinnabar of golden clouds and pearly vapors are like me; when my Way <term>Dao</term> <gloss>the path of spiritual perfection</gloss> is complete, I shall depart and ascend to heaven in broad daylight. Eighteen thousand men followed on horses.

In Lyu Xiang's Rhapsody on the Beautiful Woman <note>original: 美人賦</note>: When the Emperor first galloped into the unpredictable, he covered the four seas and became the sovereign.

Zhang Nanshi's poem mentions sensing the expedition sails rising as the wind shifts in the sails. 

Han Yu's poem "The Basin Pond" says that from now on, whenever it rains, you must remember to come and listen to the sound of rain hitting the leaves. Wang Sunzhi's "Ode to the Autumn River" describes light glinting in the twilight and distant scenery. Li Shangyin's "Fine Rain" poem writes of the Chu girl's state of mind at that time, with cool, colorful hair. Xu Hun's poem "Seeing off a Hermit" notes that there are no paths leading to the grass; since ancient times, the clouds and forests have been far from the bustle of the city. 

Xue Neng's poem says that he regrets his return date is late, as he hears the geese of the frontier. Wen Tingyun's "Opening of the Saint's Temple" poem describes the road splitting by the mountain stream, with rocks tucked amidst the misty thickets for ten miles, and old trees swaying in the wind. Fang Gan's poem notes the falling trees along the bank. Zheng Gu's poem "Loss and Alarm" asks where one can find lodging on the autumn shore when the moon is dim and the wind is fierce, amidst the yellow reeds. 

Wei Zhuang's poem "Inscribed at the Residence of Yin Xi" mentions the barren field and the autumn cypress. Lin Tong's poem mentions a coarse garment and a cloth head-covering; once he finishes gathering his books, he sighs in leisure. Wang An Shi's "Apricot Blossom" poem describes a path of weeping willows sealed by purple moss, with voices heard within the courtyard. Su Shi's poem describes brushing away white ash to reveal glowing red coals, and lying down to listen to the sound of snow beating against the window. Another poem says that in the mountains, there is only the old man with the gray beard, and for several miles, there is the music of bamboo pipes to welcome and send off guests. 

Su Zhe's "East Lake" poem says that phoenix trees grow on both banks, naturally forming a forest. Huang Tingjian's poem says that the secluded spring falls into the mountain stream, silent at night. Liu Ji's "Song of the River" says the sky is long and the water is far; where is the person, amidst the reeds and a smear of mist? 

The *Zhen Gao* <note>original: "真誥", a Taoist scripture</note> mentions the mustard seed.

The <term>di</term> sacrifice is also performed in the tenth month of winter. Winter is when the five grains have matured and all things are prepared; thus, the rite is completed by gathering together to consume food and drink. ### The Great and Small Di Sacrifices

The *External Commentary on the Book of Rites* <note>original: "Li Waizhuan"</note> states that the <term>Di</term> sacrifice establishes fixed discussions. Destroyed temples do not receive seasonal sacrifices, but every five years there are two Great Sacrifices. When a divine tablet first enters the temple, a <term>Di</term> sacrifice is performed for it. In the spring of the following year, another <term>Di</term> sacrifice is held.

### Collective Offerings to the Great Ancestor

The *Comprehensive Discussions in the White Tiger Hall* <note>original: "Baihu Tong"</note> states that the <term>Di</term> sacrifice is when the tablets from the destroyed temples are all brought together to share in the offerings to the Great Ancestor. According to the *General Meaning of the Five Classics*, Kings and Dukes have a leap month every three years, representing the minor completion of the Way of Heaven. Therefore, every three years the <term>Xia</term> <gloss>collective ancestral sacrifice</gloss> is held. The <term>Xia</term> sacrifice involves taking the tablets from temples that have not yet been moved to share in the offerings within the temple of the Great Ancestor. Every five years there are two leap months, representing the great completion of the Way of Heaven. Therefore, every five years the <term>Di</term> sacrifice is held. The <term>Di</term> sacrifice involves taking the tablets from temples that have already been moved and bringing them together for offerings in the temple. This is done to avoid forgetting the lineage of the ancestors. It maintains the succession by moving from the close relatives to the distant ones, ensuring the ancestors are not forgotten. It further states that the <term>Di</term> sacrifice reaches even those in the moved temples because it is impossible for every generation to succeed the ruler <note>referring to the limitation on how many generations of individual temples are maintained before tablets are moved to a collective space</note>.

The transformative influence within the royal domain was similar to that among the feudal lords. Poems were created based on governance. The <term>Feng</term> <gloss>Airs</gloss> and <term>Ya</term> <gloss>Odes</gloss> are connected to governance, in their breadth or narrowness. Although the king's status was noble, due to the narrow scope of governance, it was categorized under <term>Feng</term>. The creation of <term>Feng</term> and <term>Ya</term> inherently followed a pattern; it was not that after collecting these poems, they were then demoted.

The Royal Feng (Wang Feng) are poems from the royal domain, while Wei Feng are from the state of Wei.</note> is perhaps to prevent confusion with the <term>Er Nan</term> <gloss>Two Nans</gloss> <note>The "Two Nans" refer to the Airs of Zhou and the Airs of Shao, the first two sections of the Guofeng (Airs of the States) in the Shijing, traditionally associated with the virtuous governance of King Wen and King Wu of Zhou.</note>, hence the three <term>Wei</term> <gloss>Airs</gloss> are interspersed.

<term>Cao Shi Cuizhong</term> said: The composition of the <term>Chunqiu</term> <gloss>Spring and Autumn Annals</gloss> began in the first year of Duke Yin. The first year of Duke Yin was the forty-ninth year of King Ping. With no king ruling the entire realm, the new year was recorded as if it originated in Lu, thus it is said that "when the traces of the king vanished, poetry perished."

<margin></margin>
->Ji Shi Cheng said:<-
</margin>
<term>Ji Shi Cheng</term> said: What Mencius meant by "poetry perished" was the perishing of the <term>Ya</term> <gloss>Odes</gloss> and <term>Song</term> <gloss>Hymns</gloss>. Since King Ping's poems were considered <term>Guofeng</term> <gloss>Airs of the States</gloss>, they were thereby ranked among those of the feudal lords. However, the <term>Chunqiu</term> sometimes recorded "Son of Heaven" in order to preserve the kingly way.

He replied: Their words and phrases show that <term>Feng</term> mostly originated from common people, while <term>Ya</term> <gloss>Odes</gloss> were composed by scholar-officials. Although <term>Ya</term> contains criticisms, its language differs from <term>Feng</term>.

<margin></margin>

<term>Chen Shi Zhi</term> said: Most <term>Ya</term> poems were ceremonial songs for court assemblies and banquets, or were composed by high ministers and grandees for remonstrance and submission of advice. After the eastward relocation <note>Refers to the move of the Zhou capital to Luoyang in 771 BCE, marking the beginning of the Eastern Zhou Dynasty and a decline in royal authority.</note>, the court had no new compositions, and high ministers had no advice to offer, thus <term>Ya</term> poems perished. Only folk customs remained.

**History of the Tang Dynasty, Treatise on Officials:** The Office of the Imperial Supply <note>original: "鈞盾署" - an agency responsible for state provisions</note> employs two directors and four assistants, with ten supervisors. They are responsible for supplying fuel and charcoal, as well as reeds, cattails, pond items, and marsh products to provide for sacrifices, imperial audiences, and banquets for guests.

**Lu Lianzi:** Chen Wuyu said to his gatekeeper, "In the past, when the state of Chu came to attack us, not a single person died. How devoid of brave men our state is!" The gatekeeper replied, "My lord, your carriage and clothes are decorated with embroidery, yet the brave men cannot even obtain coarse green cloth to wear. You have abundant food remaining, yet the brave men do not have enough bean stalks to eat. In the halls, there are ponds of wine, yet the brave men cannot taste a single drop. Wealth is what you possess, while a disregard for death is what the brave men possess. If you do not wish to give your own light possessions to others, yet you desire to obtain what others value most, is that not difficult?"

Henceforth, I request that the slaughter of these animals be prohibited together."

At that time, Hu Zhitang had a pond for releasing captive animals <note>original: "放生池" - a Buddhist practice of setting captured animals free to accumulate merit</note> in the territory. The people of Shu competed to bring animals to the pond on the three Yuan days <note>the 15th of the first, seventh, and tenth lunar months</note>.

**Records of Mirrors and Admonitions:** To the east of Daci Temple, when the two subordinates saw this, they laughed and said, "This can truly be called a censor's admonition."

In the pond, Chen Yu wrote a quatrain at the gate, and from then on, those who released animals gradually ceased. His poem says: "They are known in the world as a flock; the people of Shu compete to send them to the release pond. Recently, you have been raising dogs and plotting against chickens; I do not believe the guard is a wild cat."

<sig>Master Zhu’s Methods of Reading</sig>

Regarding what has been said before, there are points that earlier worthies had not yet reached, which emerged from the unique insights of Master Wengong <note>A reference to Zhu Xi, whose posthumous name is Wengong.</note>. If one can truly follow and carefully observe these, without deviation, then one will exhaust the principles of things, fulfill one’s nature, cultivate the self, regulate the family, and eventually reach the point of obtaining the time to put the Way into practice, attaining the level of the sages Yao and Shun. To treat one’s people in this way all begins here. How could its merit be considered shallow? 

However, in my humble opinion, the sages and worthies of the past were not without talk of reading, but whenever they taught people to read in order to exhaust principles, it reached a point of greater urgency only with Master Wengong. The great Confucian scholars of the Guan and Luo traditions <note>Referring to the Cheng-Zhu school of Neo-Confucianism, associated with the Guan and Luo regions.</note> were also not without talk of reading methods; but the instructions to follow an orderly sequence, achieve refinement, and begin by reading easier texts first, only appeared fully with the Master. That these methods appear increasingly urgent is just like the intent behind Confucius speaking frequently of the concept of "benevolence." That they were first brought to light by him, matching the efforts of Mencius regarding the goodness of human nature and the nourishing of the vital force, is something students must especially know.

Among the things stated here, there are points already mentioned by earlier generations, but there are also insights that the former worthies did not reach, which emerge from the unique perspective of Lord Wen <note>the posthumous title of Zhu Xi, 1130–1200</note>. If one can truly follow and cautiously guard these principles without transgression, then the foundation for investigating principle, fulfilling one's nature, cultivating the self, and regulating the family—extending even to obtaining the right timing to practice the Way and elevating one's ruler and people to the level of Yao and Shun <note>legendary sage-kings of antiquity</note>—will invariably be established through this. How could the practical merit of this be considered shallow? 

Furthermore, I would suggest that while the sages and worthies of old did indeed speak of reading, the instruction for people to read books in order to investigate principle became even more urgent with Lord Wen. The great scholars of the Guan and Luo regions <note>referring to the Northern Song Neo-Confucian masters such as the Cheng brothers and Zhang Zai</note> also spoke of methods for reading, but the specific emphasis on following a set sequence, attaining refinement, and first reading what is easily understood began with the Master <note>Zhu Xi</note>. This "greater urgency" is like Confucius speaking frequently of the word "Benevolence" <note>term: Ren</note>. These initial insights are comparable to Mencius's work on the goodness of human nature and the cultivation of vital energy <note>term: Qi</note>. Students especially must not fail to understand this.

# Book of Music, Volume 36

Nothing is more harmonious and intimate than total accordance. Master Kong <note>Confucius</note> said: The former kings desired to examine the standard measures and establish the principles of ritual and righteousness. Since this was impossible without education, they established schools. The equalizing of artistic patterns <note>original: "wencai"</note> refers to the correspondence between the <term>Gong</term> <gloss>the first note of the pentatonic scale</gloss> and <term>Shang</term> <gloss>the second note</gloss> in music, much like the five colors combine to form a pattern. The former kings created music to transform the people. Because the sounds of music are harmonious, the rituals governing the close and distant are manifested in music. Because the sounds of music have clarity and turbidity, high and low pitches, the distinctions between noble and base, old and young, are manifested in music. Because the sounds of music possess <term>Yin and Yang</term> <gloss>the cosmic dualism of dark and light, female and male</gloss> and the <term>Lülü</term> <gloss>the twelve-tone system of bamboo pitch pipes</gloss>, the natural order of men and women is manifested in music.

The <note>the family name, likely referring to an earlier commentator</note> clan said: This refers to performing the artistic patterns and the ornaments of balanced sound. It begins broadly and ends with restraint. At the start of the broad portion, the longevity of the music cannot be simple; in the final restraint, the artistic patterns must be reduced. By regulating the depth of virtue, one can cause people to return to the tranquility of their original nature and not pursue the movement of external things. How then could human desires exhaust and extinguish the heavenly

<column-break/>

principles? The laws of music describe this and supplement this. The substance of music inherently possesses small and large aspects; its use inherently possesses beginning and end. To describe it with these terms of small and large means that the large and small complete each other without an imbalance of weight. To supplement it with the sequence of beginning and end means that the beginning and end generate each other without a disorder of priority. Using this to symbolize the conduct of affairs, then affairs will contain the proportions of small and large, beginning and end. If one regulates the depth of virtue to form the nature, and symbolizes the conduct of affairs to form the behavior, then the sounds of the instruments and the movements of stillness and activity—one distant and one near—allow the principle of the close and distant to reside therein. One high and one low allows the principle of the noble and base to reside therein. One first and one after allows the principle of old and young to reside therein. One internal and one external allows the principle of men and women to reside therein. How can these principles not be manifested in music? Does this not originate in the proportions of small and large within the pitch pipes?

Lu Lianzi: Chen Wuyu said to his retainers, "Formerly, when the state of Chu invaded, not a single man died for the cause. Why does our state have so few soldiers of merit?" A retainer replied, "The lord uses embroidered silks for his carriage and clothing, yet the soldiers are not even allowed to use them as trim. You have surplus food, but the soldiers do not have enough bean-stalks to eat. You have pools of wine in your halls, yet the soldiers have not tasted a drop. Wealth is what you possess, while a willingness to die is what the soldiers value. If you are unwilling to share what you possess with others, yet expect to receive what they value, is that not difficult?"

## Yellow Crane Tower

The Yellow Crane Tower is located in present-day Wuchang. The Tang Dynasty Illustrated Treatises <note>original: "Tu Jing"</note> state that Fei Wenyi <note>a legendary figure often identified with the immortal Fei Yi</note> ascended to immortality and rode a yellow crane back to rest at this spot. Zhang Nanxuan <note>the Song dynasty scholar Zhang Shi</note> said that the Yellow Crane Tower was named after the mountain. Near the current Yellow Crane Tower, there is a mountain named Yellow Swan <note>term: Huanggu</note>. Nanxuan’s explanation is correct. Regarding the swan <note>term: gu</note>, Cai Heng says that many phoenixes are white, and these are called <term>gu</term> <gloss>swans</gloss>. The Suoyin commentary <note>a commentary on the Records of the Grand Historian</note> says that the <term>hong</term> <gloss>wild goose</gloss> and <term>gu</term> <gloss>swan</gloss> are a single type of bird, much like the male and female phoenix <note>term: fenghuang</note>. Therefore, the swan is of the phoenix species. It is sometimes called "great" <note>term: hong</note>, sometimes "white," and sometimes "yellow." Yellow and white are similar colors. "Great" refers to its size. The commentary on the Superintendent of Furs <note>a section of the Rites of Zhou</note> says that the swan refers to a small bird among the geese that is difficult to hit with an arrow. The Jade Chapters <note>term: Yupian, an early dictionary</note> state that the <term>yangu</term> <gloss>goose-swan</gloss> is a swan; it is a bird that knows what is coming. The "spiritual swan" of today is this goose-swan.

# The Guoyu on the Establishment of the Pitch Standard

## To Determine Measurements: The Ancient Blind Musicians Evaluated the Central Pitch, Measured it, and Created the System of Pitch Standards and Bell Calibration

### Using the Central Pitch to Determine the Pitch Standard, and Using the Pitch Standard to Establish the Calibration of the Bells

The <term>Jia Shu</term> <gloss>The Commentary by Jia Gongyan</gloss> cites the <term>Guoyu</term> <gloss>Discourses of the States</gloss> to explain that in determining the size [of the pipes], one must ensure they correspond to the pitch standards. The "central pitch" refers to the generation of the upper and lower notes, which determines the length of the pitch pipes. "Measuring the pitch standard" refers to calculating by the pipes. Establishing the calibration of the bells based on doubling or halving [the pipe length] is what determines the length of the corresponding pitch pipes. Regarding this: examining the original meaning of the <term>Guoyu</term>, it means examining the central pitch to create the <term>Huangzhong</term> pipe. "Measuring it" refers to carefully inspecting the consistency of the central pitch. "Measuring the pitch standard" means that once the dimensions of the <term>Huangzhong</term> are obtained, one then measures the fractions of the upper and lower generations to determine the short and long dimensions of the twelve pitch pipes. "Calibrating the bells" refers to establishing the standard calibration based on the pitch pipes, in order to tune the sounds of the twelve pitch pipes and the bells.

# The Discourses of the States: The pitches are that by which the standard scales are established.

## They emerge from measurement. The spirit-blind musicians of antiquity examined the middle tones and measured them with standardized systems to regulate the pitches and the tuning of the bells.

### Using the middle tones to fix the pitches, and using the pitches to establish the standard scale for the bells.

Jia’s Commentary <note>referring to the scholar Jia Gongyan</note> cites the Discourses of the States <note>original: "Guoyu"</note> because he wishes to show that the size of the instruments must correspond to the pitches. "Middle tones" refers to the upward and downward generation that determines the length of the pitch pipes. "Measuring the pitches" means calculating the pitches based on the standard pipes, using the principle of doubling or halving the length to establish the scale of the bells. This ensures they correspond to the length of the pitch pipes. According to the original meaning of the Discourses of the States, "examining the middle tones" refers to creating the Yellow Bell pipe. "Measuring them" means carefully observing the standard measure of the middle tones. "Measuring the pitches" means that once the dimensions of the Yellow Bell are obtained, one calculates the fractions for upward and downward generation to determine the lengths of the twelve pitch pipes. "Tuning the bells" means establishing the scale based on the pitch pipes to harmonize the sounds of the twelve pitches and the two types of bells.

From this point onward, Shun should have established his own temple for the Cultural Ancestor <note>The term refers to a deified ancestor or predecessor, specifically associated with Yao's lineage in this context</note>. The shrine of Yao's Cultural Ancestor ought to have been transferred to the territory of Dan Zhu.

## The Great Counsel of Yu: On the first day of the first month, he received the mandate at the Divine Ancestor Temple

**The Correct Meaning:** The *Canon of Shun* states that at the beginning of his reign, Shun reported his accession to the Cultural Ancestor. This passage suggests that if Shun knew he was receiving the mandate at the very start, it was effectively the same as reporting the completion of his tenure <note>In Confucian ritual logic, accepting power involves informing the ancestors; 'receiving' and 'reporting the end' are ritually linked concepts here</note>. The "Divine Ancestor" is equivalent to the aforementioned "Cultural Ancestor." Thus, the tradition says that the transmission of the mandate regarding the conclusion of duties occurred at the ancestral temples of the Cultural and Divine Ancestors, calling them "Divine" to signify their reverence.

### The Mandate Received Is Equivalent to the Command Concerning Shun's Final Duties: The Divine Ancestor

The Divine Ancestor corresponds to Shun's founding ancestor. According to the *Imperial Genealogy*:
The Yellow Emperor begot Changyi.
Changyi begot Zhuanxu.
Zhuanxu begot Qiongchan.
Qiongchan begot Jingkang.
Jingkang begot Goumang.
Goumang begot Qiaoniu.
Qiaoniu begot Gusou.
Gusou begot Shun.

This establishes that Shun had seven generations of ancestors in his temple system, with the Yellow Emperor serving as the founding ancestor. Therefore, the term "Cultural Ancestor" (Wen Zu) and "Divine Ancestor" (Shen Zong) refer to the same reality under different names. The word "Ancestor" in "Cultural Ancestor" highlights civil virtue, while "Divine" in "Divine Ancestor" emphasizes spiritual reverence.

**Commentary:** The four types of metal instruments are all used in military and hunting contexts. In military affairs, the drum comes first and the metal instruments follow. This is recorded in the office of the Grand Marshal.

They harmonize with the drum. The **zhuo** <gloss>a small bell-shaped bronze instrument</gloss> is the same as the *zheng* <gloss>a bronze warning gong</gloss>. Its form is like a small bell, and its sound is deep and resonant. When spoken of in terms of its sound, it is called *zhuo*; when spoken of in terms of its function of alerting people, it is called *zheng*. In truth they are one and the same. **It is sounded when the army is on the march**, to serve as a marker for the drumbeat. <margin>Ma Duanlin says: In the *Odes*, "the zheng-men strike and the drums sound"; when spoken of in terms of correcting people, the *dingning* is called *zheng*. In truth they are one and the same.</margin> According to the office of the Marshal: when the army marches, the *zhuo* is sounded. <margin>Jia's sub-commentary: that refers to the Duke's army.</margin> The **nao** <gloss>a hand-held bronze bell without a clapper</gloss> is like a bell, but without a clapper; it has a handle and is held and sounded, used to halt the beating of drums. According to the office of the Marshal: the *nao* is sounded and the troops withdraw. <margin>Jia's sub-commentary: when advancing, the drum is beaten; when retreating, the nao is sounded.</margin> The **duo** <gloss>a large bell with a clapper</gloss> is a large bell. It is rung to transmit the signal to beat the drums. According to the office of the Marshal: the Marshal rings the *duo*. <margin>Jia's sub-commentary: this has a metal clapper in a metal body, so it is called the "metal *duo*"; in the army, this metal bell with metal clapper is rung. The one with a wooden clapper is the "wooden *duo*", rung when issuing commands.</margin> When the two Marshals ring the *duo*, the army commanders and those below immediately beat the drums, hence it is said to transmit the drum signal.

# Volume One Hundred and Seventy

The spirit tablets of destroyed temples and those not yet destroyed are all brought together to share offerings at the Great Ancestor's temple. This occurs every five years in what is called the "Grand Sacrifice" (*Yin Ji*).

According to the old Han system, there was a *Di* sacrifice every three years. Spirit tablets from destroyed temples were combined for offerings at the High Temple (the temple of the founding emperor), while spirit tablets from extant temples had never been combined for sacrifice.

In the fifth year of the Yuan Shi era [1 CE], the *Di* sacrifice was first instituted. Eighteen years prior, the Emperor had personally visited Chang'an and performed this rite.

The word *Di* signifies "scrutiny" or "verification," establishing the meanings of seniority, juniority, honor, and humility through the order of generations. The *Di* sacrifice is held in the fourth month of summer. In summer, Yang energy is above and Yin energy is below; thus, the correct principles of seniority and humility are established. The *Di* sacrifice is also held in the tenth month of winter. In winter, the five grains mature, items are complete, and rites are fulfilled; thus, they gather for communal dining. This canonical practice has been suspended for eight years. We request that it be reinstated according to ritual propriety and implemented at the appropriate time.

### *Di*: Grand *Di*, Minor *Di*

**Ritual Outer Commentary:** *Di* means to scrutinize.

**Determining the Proposal:** The Emperor followed the proposal. Since then, the *Di* sacrifice has been fixed as grand, while other sacrifices are considered minor. The Spring and Autumn Annals contain references to *Di* but not to the specific minor form. Destroyed temples have no seasonal sacrifices; they only participate in the two Grand Sacrifices every five years. When a spirit tablet enters the temple, a preliminary *Di* is held first. The following spring, another *Di* is performed, and then another yearly *Di* follows.

### Sharing Offerings at the Great Ancestor's Temple

**Comprehensive White Tiger Hall:** Those performing the *Di* combine the spirit tablets of destroyed temples to share offerings at the Great Ancestor's temple.

**Examination:** According to the *General Principles of the Five Classics*: For kings and feudal lords, three years constitute one intercalation cycle. This completes the lesser way of Heaven. Therefore, the *Xia* sacrifice is held every three years. The *Xia* takes the spirit tablets of untransferred temples and combines them for offerings in the Great Ancestor's temple. Five years constitute two intercalations, completing the greater way of Heaven. Therefore, the *Di* sacrifice is held every five years. The *Di* takes the spirit tablets of already transferred temples and combines them for offerings in the temple. This ensures we do not forget the physical lineage of our ancestors, maintaining their succession from close relatives to distant ones, ensuring we never forget our forebears. It is also said that the *Di* extends to transferred temples because descendants cannot succeed as sovereigns generation after generation indefinitely.

that which has already been stated by <term>Wen Gong</term> <gloss>Master Zhu Xi</gloss>, there are insights not reached by former sages but arising from his unique vision. If one can indeed strictly follow and carefully observe these methods, without any transgression, then investigating principles to the utmost, fulfilling one's nature, cultivating the self, and regulating the family, up to obtaining the right time to carry out the Way and reaching the level of Yao and Shun, will all find their foundation here. Can such merit and utility be considered shallow?

However, I humbly submit that ancient sages did not refrain from speaking about reading; yet it was only with Wen Gong that the teaching of people to read for the purpose of <term>qiong li</term> <gloss>investigating principles</gloss> became more urgent. Likewise, the great Confucians of Guanxi and Luoyang <note>referring to Zhang Zai and the Cheng brothers</note> did not refrain from discussing methods of reading; yet the specific emphasis on proceeding in sequence and attaining thoroughness, and the advice to begin with what is easily understood, first appeared explicitly through the instruction of this Teacher [Zhu Xi]. This increasing urgency is like Confucius's frequent elaboration on the concept of "humaneness" <gloss>Ren</gloss>. Initially perceived as identical to Mencius's work on innate goodness and nourishing the vital energy <gloss>Qi</gloss>, this insight is especially necessary for scholars to understand.

What has already been said by former worthies, there are also points that former worthies never reached and that emerged from Master Wengong's own insight. If one can truly follow these instructions with certainty, guard them with care, and never overstep them, then the investigation of principle to the utmost, the full realization of one's nature, the cultivation of the person, the ordering of the household, and even the obtaining of the proper time to put the Way into practice, reaching to the utmost in making one's ruler and people like Yao and Shun: all of this has its foundation here. How could its efficacy be shallow?

Moreover, I would venture to say that from ancient times the sages and worthies did not fail to speak about reading. But in teaching people to read in order to investigate principle, it became more urgent and pointed with Master Wengong. The great Confucians of the Guan and Luo schools likewise did not fail to speak about the method of reading. But as for arriving at the ordered progression that attains refinement, and the saying that one should first read what is easy to understand, these appeared first with the Master.

That it became more urgent and pointed is like Confucius speaking often of the word "humaneness." That it appeared for the first time is like Mencius's achievement in speaking of the goodness of human nature and the nourishing of the vital force. Students especially cannot afford not to know this.

# Book of Music, Volume 36

Harmonious and compliant: none are not intimate. Master Kong says: "The former kings wished to examine [things] through measures and numbers, and regulate them through rites and righteousness; this could not be achieved without teaching. Therefore, they established schools." "Literary pattern" refers to the correspondence of notes in music, like five colors forming a design. The former kings used music to transform the people. Because musical tones are harmonized, the rites distinguishing close from distant relatives are seen in music. Because musical tones have clarity and turbidity, high and low pitches, the status of noble and base, and age differences between elders and juniors, are seen in music. Because musical tones have Yin and Yang, Lü and Lü (pitch pipes), the principles governing men and women are seen in music.

<margin>Commentary:</margin> Beginning with "performing literary patterns," this section decorates sounds. It starts broadly and ends concisely. At the beginning of breadth, one cannot end long-lasting joy with plainness. In the ending of conciseness, one must reflect on literary patterns. By using these to constrain virtue’s depth, one can enable people to return to the stillness of their nature and not chase the movement of external things. How then can human desires be exhausted or heavenly principle destroyed?

<column-break/>

Principle has its regulations; those who narrate this follow them. Those who assist this do so accordingly. The substance of music indeed has size, and its function indeed has beginning and end. Narrating it with terms of large and small ensures that big and small complement each other without imbalance in weight. Assisting it with the order of beginning and end ensures that beginnings and endings generate each other without disorder in sequence. Using this to image affairs and actions means that affairs and actions will naturally possess magnitude and temporal structure. Constraining virtue’s depth serves as the essence of nature; imaging affairs and actions serves as conduct. Thus, sound and voice transcend boundaries, while movement and stillness take form. One far, one near, and the principle of kinship remains therein. One high, one low, and the principle of nobility remains therein. One senior, one junior, and the principle of age remains therein. One inner, one outer, and the principle of gender remains therein. How can we ensure these principles all manifest in music? Is it not rooted in the naming of large and small through pitch pipes?

# Book of Music, Volume 36

Harmony and accord; none fail to be harmonious and affectionate. Master Kong said: The former kings wished to examine it through measures and numbers, and regulate it through ritual and rightness. Without teaching this cannot be done, so they established schools and grades. Pattern and color mean that the musical notes gong and shang correspond to one another, just as the five colors form a pattern. The former kings created music to transform the people. Because musical sounds are harmonious and blended, the principle of intimacy and distance is made visible in music. Because musical sounds have clarity and turbidity, high and low, the distinctions of noble and base, elder and younger are made visible in music. Because musical sounds have yin and yang, pitch-pipes and pitch-standards, the principle of man and woman is made visible in music.

Master Cheng said: That is, the ornament of performing pattern and color and balancing the sounds begins broadly and ends with restraint. Beginning broadly, the extended music must not be left unadorned. Ending with restraint, the pattern and color must not be left unexamined. To use this as a plumb-line for the fullness of virtue is to enable people to return to the stillness of their nature and not pursue the movement of things. How then could one exhaust human desires and destroy heavenly principle? The pitch-pipes describe this; these assist this. The substance of music inherently has small and great; its function inherently has beginning and end. Describing it through these designations of small and great, then the small and great complete one another without any inequality of light and heavy. Assisting it through the order of beginning and end, then beginning and end generate one another without any disorder of before and after. Using this to represent affairs and conduct, then affairs may contain small and great, beginning and end. Plumb-line the fullness of virtue to form the nature; represent affairs and conduct to form the conduct. Then, transmitted through sound, given form through movement and stillness, one far and one near, the principle of intimacy and distance resides therein. One above and one below, the principle of noble and base resides therein. One before and one after, the principle of elder and younger resides therein. One within and one without, the principle of man and woman resides therein. How could it be that these principles do not all manifest visibly in music? Does this not originate from the designations of small and great in the pitch-pipes?

First is "remonstrance by hint" (諷諫). This is exemplified by Confucius.
<note>Case in point: In the *Gongyang Commentary* for Duke Ding, Year 12, it says that when Confucius heard that the Ji clan was acting presumptuously, he told Ji Sun: "A household should not store armor; a town should not have walls of one hundred *zhi*. Second is "remontance by compliance" or "smooth remonstrance" (順諫). This is exemplified by Cao Ji.
<note>Case in point: This refers to the remonstrance against Cao mentioned above.</note>

Third is "direct remonstrance" (直諫). This is exemplified by Zi Jia Ju.
<note>Case in point: In the *Gongyang Commentary* for Duke Zhao, Year 25, it says: "Zi Jia Ju said: 'The ministers have long usurped the privileges of the Son of Heaven; this is not respecting the ruler's prerogatives.'"</note>

Fourth is "contentious remonstrance" or "remontance by dispute" (爭諫). This is exemplified by Zi Fan requesting to return.
<note>Case in point: In the *Gongyang Commentary* for Duke Xuan, Year 15, it says: King Zhuang of Chu besieged Song. Inside the city, Zi Fan and Hua Yuan climbed onto the siege mounds to speak with each other. Hua Yuan said to Zi Fan: "We exchange children to eat them and break bones to burn as fuel." Zi Fan replied to Hua Yuan: "My army has only seven days' worth of grain." So Zi Fan persuaded the King of Chu to also withdraw. When frequent remonstrations were not heard, he led his troops away, and the King of Chu also returned.</note>

Fifth is "simple-minded remonstrance" or "naive remonstrance" (戇諫).

# Volume 24

The *yu* <term>敔</term> is shaped like a lacquered bamboo tube with a narrowed mouth. It has a circumference of two *wei* <gloss>units of measurement for girth</gloss>, a length of five chi six cun, and is covered with goat skin. It has two handles. The "sparse painting" refers to the patterns drawn on it; we infer this from Han dynasty regulations. Zheng Xuan’s note on the "Towel Carriage" chapter states that the color of the *zhu* <term>柷</term> is more red than black. The commentary explains that "sparse painting" means the designs are widely spaced and painted. Zi Chun <note>Zi Chun: A commentator identified in later tradition as Du Zizhi or possibly another scholar from the Han era, cited by Zheng Xuan.</note> reads *yuan* (far) as *dang* (wash), taking it from the phrase in the "Special Sacrifice for Heaven" chapter: "When the smell and taste have not yet formed, wash away its sound." He argues that this refers to the blowing of the five-holed bamboo flute (*sui*) of his time, and the later scholars follow this view.

It says "standing," which refers to the *zhu* music. The *zhu* is used in Xia dynasty music because the Bell Master had *zhu* music. Since this *zhu* music corresponds to theirs, we know that the *zhu* music taught here is the *zhu* music created during the Xia dynasty. If the Sheng Master teaches it, then these three instruments must be located in the courtyard. This can be inferred because if they were near the hall, the other instruments would also be there; but since the sheng pipes are under the hall, and distant from the hall places them in the courtyard, their location in the courtyard is known.

<column-break/>

They are blown at specific times. In winter, Water rules; the number of Water is six. Six times seven equals forty-two, so the length of the *yu* likely derives from this principle. The *sheng* <term>笙</term> has thirteen reeds. The *Guangya* <note>Guangya: An ancient Chinese dictionary/encyclopedia compiled by Zhang Yi during the Three Kingdoms period.</note> says the *sheng* is made from gourd, with thirteen pipes; the main pipe is on the left side. The *yu* <term>竽</term> resembles this but has thirty-six pipes, with the main pipe in the center. The *Li Tu* <note>Li Tu: Illustrated Canon of Rituals, a work describing ritual objects and procedures.</note> says the *yu* is four chi two cun long. Here, the *yu* has thirty-six reeds, which matches the *Li Tu*.

Regarding the *chi* <term>篪</term> having seven holes: The *Guangya* says the *chi* is made of bamboo, one chi four cun long, with eight holes; one hole protrudes three fen above the surface. The *Li Tu* says the *chi* has nine holes. The Minister of Agriculture <note>Minister of Agriculture: Also known as Si Nong, referring to the scholar Zheng Zhong.</note> says it has seven holes, but this is likely an error by the copyist; it should say eight holes. Alternatively, the Minister of Agriculture may have had a different source.

In spring, the *du* <term>牘</term> uses bamboo five or six cun thick, seven chi long, or shorter ones one or two chi long. At its end are two holes. The *zhu* is shaped such that both hands strike the ground [to play it]. Its length is six chi five cun, and it contains a mallet inside.

## Yellow Crane Tower

Yellow Crane Tower is located in present-day Wuchang. The Tang Dynasty *Tujing* (Geographical Record) states: "Fei Wenwei ascended to immortality, rode a yellow crane back, and rested here." Zhang Nanxuan said: "The name 'Yellow Crane' comes from the mountain. Today, beside Yellow Crane Tower there is a mountain named Huanghu (Yellow Swan). This explanation by Nanxuan is correct."

According to Cai Heng: "Among phoenixes, those with much white are called hu (swan/geese-like birds)." The *Suoyin* commentary says: "Honghu (great swan) and hu are one type of bird. If we consider the phoenix, then hu belongs to the phoenix class." Some call it Hong (great), some Bai (white), some Huang (yellow). Note that yellow is close to white. Hong means "great." A note on the *Qiu* chapter states: "Hu refers to Yanhu (wild goose/swan), which are small birds difficult to hit." The * Yupian* dictionary defines Yanhu as hu, a bird known for coming [with the seasons]. Today, Linghu is considered to be Yanhu.

## Yellow Crane Tower

The Yellow Crane Tower is in present-day Wuchang. The Tang-era illustrated gazetteer states that Fei Wenhui ascended to immortality, rode a yellow crane, and returned to rest here. Zhang Nanxuan says the Yellow Crane is named after the mountain. Beside the present Yellow Crane Tower there is a mountain called Yellow Swan, so Nanxuan's explanation is correct. Consider the swan: Cai Heng says that among phoenixes, those that are mostly white are called swans. The <term>Suoyin</term> <gloss>Seeking the Hidden</gloss> commentary says the grand swan is a single bird, like the phoenix. The commentary on the <term>Si Qiu</term> <gloss>Master of Fur Robes</gloss> says the swan-goose is a small bird among swans that is difficult to hit. The <term>Yupian</term> <gloss>Jade Chapters dictionary</gloss> says the swan-goose is a swan, a bird that knows what is coming. The present-day spirit-swan is the swan-goose.

As for sacrificing to worthy predecessors in the Western School or honoring the ancestors of music in the Hall of Blind Masters, the transmitters also say that sacrifices are offered at the school where one studies. However, the Duke of Zhou and Confucius were not possessions exclusively belonging to Zhou or Lu. If separate masters were established for each classic, how could such a practice exist in the canonical rites of Zhou?

In antiquity, the people regarded their ruler as their teacher. Benevolence, lowliness, longevity, and early death—these were truly governed by the ruler, while ministers assisted and guided him. The ruler was the one who taught and protected the myriad people. Before Confucius, those called "sages" or "worthies," those possessing the Way or virtue, invariably held high positions during their lives and received major sacrificial honors after their deaths. This was not something mere students could claim.

### 靜悅 (Quiet Joy)
Emperor Yang of Sui, in his letter to Yán Zhìyǐ: "Discipline upheld with solemn cultivation; the gate of Dharma is quiet and joyful."

---

### 靜嘉 (Quiet and Fine)
>The *Book of Songs*: "What did he announce? The dishes were quiet and fine."
>Zhang Heng, *Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital*: "Washed and cleansed, quiet and fine; the rites and ceremonies clearly distinguished."

---

### 靜勝 (Quiet Overcoming)
Yang Ling on the great sound: "The faintest sound is quiet and overcoming, truly in accord with the human heart; the primal unity far matches the **music of nature**."

Also, from the *New History of the Five Dynasties*, "Treatise on the Offices of the Provinces": Yaozhou was originally Huayuan County; at the end of the Tang it belonged to Li Maozhen, who established it as Yaozhou and stationed the Yisheng Army there. In the time of Emperor Mo of Liang, Li Maozhen's son Wen Tao surrendered the prefecture to Liang; Liang changed Yaozhou to Chongzhou, and "Yisheng" was called "Quiet Overcoming." Also, Wan Changgeng.

---

### 理茸 (Lǐróng)
From a hall record: "Yang Renshu of Geshan, a Yellow-Cap master <note>a Daoist priest</note>, knew what was meant by *lǐróng*."

Also, Zhang Yue wrote a poem on the Lǐróng Temple of Longshan.

---

### 靜朗 (Quiet and Bright)
*The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons*: "Water stands still to serve as a mirror; fire is quiet and bright."

---

### 靜厚 (Quiet and Generous)
Su Shi, "Inscribed on Yuke's Bamboo": "Wherever Yuke went, poetry was on his lips and bamboo in his hands. His countenance was stern and cold, such that the quiet and cautious, the restless and the generous, the petty and the shallow could all be moved. Now, though we are separated by a thousand *li*, his poetry may still be sought, and his bamboo may still be begged for. Yet the quiet and generous one among them cannot be reached: this is why, seeing the bamboo, this man sighs."

The Tang dynasty dances *Anle* (Peaceful Joy), *Taiping* (Great Peace), *Pozhen* (Breaking the Formation), *Qingshan* (Celebrating Goodness), *Dading* (Great Stability), *Shangyuan* (Upper Primordial), *Shengshou* (Holy Longevity), and *Guangsheng* (Illuminating Sages) all used thunderous large drums accompanied by music from Kucha <note>original: "龜茲"</note>. For the *Dading* music, gold gongs were added. Only the *Qingshan* dance exclusively used the music of the Western Liang dynasty. Formerly, the three dances *Pozhen*, *Shangyuan*, and *Qingshan* had their costumes and headdresses altered to harmonize with bell and chime instruments <note>referring to court ritual music</note>, and were presented separately at suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples. The *Pozhen* was designated as the martial dance representing the Seven Virtues, while the *Qingshan* served as the civil dance representing the Nine Merits. Since Empress Wu’s usurpation and disorder led to the destruction of the Tang ancestral temples, these rituals ultimately fell into disuse. According to the *Treatise on Calendars and Ritual Music*, the Yellow Bell (*Huangzhong*) represents the Heavenly Unity, with a pipe length of nine inches. The Forest Bell (*Linzhong*) represents the Earthly Unity, with a pipe length of six inches. The Great Cluster (*Dacuxi*)<note>OCR reads "Da Zu", likely a misprint for Da Cuxi (Great Cluster)</note> represents the Human Unity, with a pipe length of eight inches. It also states that the twelve pipes generate one another; all follow the pattern of ascending by eight and descending by two. The generation ends in the middle tone. The *lü* (pipes) and *lv* (tubes), representing *yin* and *yang*, originate from the Yellow Bell. They begin with a leftward rotation. The phrase "eight times eight forms the position" means: suppose the Yellow Bell generates the Forest Bell; this involves passing through eight positions. From here on down, this is the same; thus "eight times eight forms the position."

# Guoyu: The Purpose of Establishing the Lü

## To Determine Measures: Ancient Blind Masters Assessed the Central Tone and Measured It to Establish the System of Lü and Tune the Bells

### This means using the central tone to establish the lü, and using the lü to establish the tuning of the bells.

The commentary by Jia Xuan quotes the *Guoyu* because the size of the bell must correspond to the pitch of the lü. The "central tone" refers to the upward and downward generations used to determine the length of the pipes. One measures the lü by calculating their lengths based on doubling or halving to tune the bells, which corresponds to the proper lengths of the lü. According to the original meaning of the *Guoyu*, "assessing the central tone" means determining the dimensions of the Yellow Bell pipe; "measuring it" means carefully examining the standard measure of the central tone. "Measuring the lü" means that once the dimension of the Yellow Bell is obtained, one then determines the fractions for upward and downward generation to fix the shortness or length of the twelve lü pipes. "Tuning the bells" means establishing the tuning based on the lü pipes to harmonize the sounds of the twelve lü and the twelve bronze bells.

# The <term>Guoyu</term> <gloss>Discourses of the States</gloss>: The pitch pipes are that by which the <term>jun</term> <gloss>tuning standard</gloss> is established

## and measures are set forth. The ancient blind music masters examined the central tones and measured them to establish the pitch pipes and tune the bells, meaning

### they used the central tones to fix the pitch pipes, and used the pitch pipes to establish the tuning standard of the bells.

Jia's subcommentary cites the <term>Guoyu</term>: it wishes to take the great and small as that which must correspond to the pitch pipes and be in harmony. "Central tones" refers to the ascending and descending generation. Fixing the lengths of the pitch pipes and measuring the pipes by means of the pipes, establishing the tuning standard of the bells from double and half. That is, corresponding to the lengths of the pitch pipes. In the original meaning of the <term>Guoyu</term>, it says: examine the central tones in order to fashion the Yellow Bell pipe. "Measuring it" means carefully investigating the exact measure of the central tones. "Measuring the pipes" means: having obtained the degree-numbers of the Yellow Bell, one then measures its ascending-generation and descending-generation fractions in order to fix the lengths of the twelve pitch pipes. "Tuning the bells" means: on the basis of the pitch pipes one establishes the tuning standard in order to attune the sounds of the twelve pitch pipes and the two bells.
